analogy.p: You cannot drink the whole pot to check the flavour, so you stir it and taste one spoonful. Stirring is like random sampling (every part has an equal chance of being tasted), the spoonful is the quadrat, and tasting several spoonfuls is repeating to get a reliable mean. A transect is like tasting spoonfuls at regular depths from top to bottom to see how the flavour changes. The analogy breaks down because soup is mixed evenly, whereas organisms in a habitat are patchy, so many more samples are needed.

bullets: **Population** = all the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time. **Community** = all the populations of different species living together in a habitat.
**Abundance** can be given as a count (number per square metre) or as **percentage cover** (the % of the ground a plant covers).

**Distribution** is explained by looking for links with **abiotic factors** (light intensity, temperature, soil moisture, soil pH, wind speed, mineral content of soil) and **biotic factors** (competition, grazing, predation, disease).

The AQA required practical asks you to **measure the population size of a common species in a habitat** and **use sampling techniques to investigate the effect of a factor on the distribution of this species**.
A good sample must be **representative** of the whole habitat, otherwise the estimate will be biased and the conclusion unreliable.
Typical species used: daisies, dandelions, plantain, buttercups or clover in a lawn or field, because they are common, easy to see, easy to identify and do not move.
core.h: Why ecologists sample: distribution and abundance
core.p: An ecologist cannot count every single organism in a habitat, because there are far too many and many of them move, hide or are tiny. Instead we **sample**: we study a small, carefully chosen part of the habitat and use it to estimate what is happening in the whole. The two things we usually want to know are the **abundance** (how many individuals of a species there are, or how much of the area it covers) and the **distribution** (where in the habitat the species is found, and why it is found there and not elsewhere).

bullets: Area of a square quadrat = side x side. For a 0.5 m quadrat: 0.5 x 0.5 = **0.25 m2**.
Quadrats are best for **plants and slow-moving or non-moving animals** (for example snails, limpets or daisies) that stay put while you count them.

Lay the quadrat flat on the ground and count only the organisms of the target species inside the frame. Decide beforehand a rule for plants touching the edge, for example count a plant if it is more than half inside, or count only those touching the top and left edges.
Use the same quadrat size every time so the results are comparable.
Identify the species using a **key** or identification guide so you are counting the right plant each time.
Do not trample the area you are about to sample, because that would damage the plants and change the data.
core.h: The quadrat: what it is and how to use it
core.p: A **quadrat** is a square frame, usually made of wood, metal or plastic, that marks out a known area of ground so that organisms inside it can be counted. Common sizes are 0.5 m by 0.5 m (area 0.25 m2) and 1 m by 1 m (area 1 m2). Some quadrats are divided into a grid of smaller squares using string, which helps with estimating percentage cover. Using a quadrat of a known area is what allows us to scale up the count to an estimate for the whole habitat.

bullets: **Step 1:** Mark out the area to be sampled by laying two long tape measures at right angles along two sides of the area, to make the axes of a grid.
**Step 2:** Use a **random number generator** (calculator, spreadsheet or random-number table) to produce two numbers, which are the x and y coordinates, for example (6, 4).
**Step 3:** Walk to the coordinates (without trampling the area), and place the quadrat there with the corner at that point.
**Step 4:** Count the number of the target species inside the quadrat and record it in a results table.
**Step 5:** Repeat steps 2 to 4 many times (at least 10 quadrats; more is better) to get a large sample.
**Step 6:** Calculate the **mean** number per quadrat, then scale up to estimate the population size of the whole area.
Why not throw the quadrat over your shoulder? It is not truly random, because it is affected by where you stand and how you throw, and it is not repeatable.
core.p: To avoid bias, the position of each quadrat must be chosen **randomly**. If you chose spots by eye you would tend to pick places with lots of the plant you are looking for, which would over-estimate the population. Random sampling gives every part of the area an equal chance of being sampled, so the sample is representative. Mark scheme answers expect the idea of **random coordinates** and **repeating**.

bullets: Random sampling **removes bias** and makes the sample representative of the whole area.
**More quadrats** gives a more reliable mean and a more accurate estimate of the true population.
A **small sample** might by chance land in an unusually dense or sparse patch, giving a misleading result.
Repeating allows an **anomaly** (a result that does not fit the pattern) to be identified, and it can be excluded from the mean (and the exclusion justified).
Sampling can only ever give an **estimate**; the true population size is unknown unless every organism is counted.
The area sampled should be large enough to include the whole habitat variation, and the quadrats spread across it.
core.h: Why random? Sample size, bias and reliability
core.p: Several words are used to judge the quality of a sampling investigation. **Bias** means the results are pushed systematically in one direction, for example by choosing quadrat positions that look nice. **Reliability** (repeatability) means that if the investigation were repeated, similar results would be obtained. A larger sample (more quadrats) is more reliable because a few unusual quadrats have less effect on the mean, and an anomalous result is easier to spot.

bullets: **Mean = total number counted / number of quadrats.**
**Mean number per m2 = mean per quadrat / area of one quadrat (m2).** For a 0.25 m2 quadrat this is the same as multiplying by 4.
**Estimated population = mean number per m2 x total area of habitat (m2).**
Example: 10 quadrats of 0.25 m2 give a total of 50 plants. Mean = 50 / 10 = 5 per quadrat. Per m2 = 5 / 0.25 = 20. In a 600 m2 field: 20 x 600 = **12 000 plants**.
If a 1 m2 quadrat is used then the mean per quadrat is already the mean per m2.
The answer is an **estimate**, so it is sensible to give it to a suitable number of significant figures.
Median = middle value when the counts are placed in order; mode = most common value. Range = highest minus lowest value, which shows how spread out the data are.
core.h: Estimating population size from quadrat data
core.p: Once you have the counts you calculate the mean number of organisms per quadrat, convert this to a number per square metre, and then multiply by the total area of the habitat. This works because we assume the sample is representative, so the density (number per m2) in the quadrats is the same as in the whole habitat. This is a common calculation in the exam and the working should always be shown.

bullets: **Percentage cover = (number of squares covered / total number of squares) x 100.**
Example: a 5 x 5 grid has 25 squares. If the plant covers 8 of them: 8 / 25 x 100 = **32%**.
Percentage cover is a measure of abundance that does not require counting individual organisms.
It is quicker, but it is a more subjective estimate, so use the same person or a clear rule for deciding.
It is useful for comparing areas, for example % cover of moss in a shady area compared with a sunny area.
Mean percentage cover is calculated across all quadrats in the same way as a mean count.
core.p: Some plants, such as grass, moss or clover, grow so densely or so spread out that individual plants cannot be counted. In these cases we estimate **percentage cover**: the percentage of the area inside the quadrat that is covered by the species. A quadrat divided into a grid of equal squares makes this easier, because you count the squares that are covered (or count a square if the plant covers more than half of it).

bullets: **Step 1:** Lay a long tape measure in a straight line across the habitat, starting where the factor you are investigating is at one extreme (for example under dense tree cover).
**Step 2:** Place a quadrat at the start (0 m), then at regular intervals (for example every 2 m or 5 m) along the line.
**Step 3:** At each position count the organisms (or estimate percentage cover) of the target species.
**Step 4:** At each position also **measure the abiotic factor** (for example light intensity or soil moisture).
**Step 5:** Repeat the whole transect at several different places and calculate means for each distance, to make the data more reliable.
A **line transect** records only organisms touching the line; a **belt transect** uses quadrats next to each other or at intervals along the line, which gives more data.
Transects show a **pattern or trend**; random quadrats show overall abundance. Use a transect when there is a clear gradient in the habitat.
core.p: Random sampling tells you how many organisms there are but not how their numbers change from place to place. To investigate how the **distribution** of a species changes across a habitat, for example from the edge of a wood out into an open field, a **transect** is used. A transect is a line (usually a long tape measure) laid across the habitat along an environmental gradient. Sampling is **systematic** rather than random, because quadrats are placed at regular intervals along the line.

bullets: Independent variable: the abiotic factor or the distance from a feature (for example distance from a tree, a hedge or a path).
Dependent variable: **number of organisms per quadrat** (or % cover), the measure of abundance.
Control variables: the **same quadrat size**, the same species being counted, the same time of day and season, the same person counting, and the same sampling method.
Compare two areas by taking an equal number of random quadrats in each, then comparing the means.
A pattern, such as more daisies as light intensity increases, shows a **correlation**; it does not prove that light is the cause because other factors may differ.
Explain the pattern using biology: plants in shade receive less light so photosynthesise less, produce less glucose and grow less, so fewer plants may survive there.
Look at the data for trends, and suggest which factor is the most likely cause, giving reasons.
core.h: Investigating the effect of a factor on distribution (required practical)
core.p: In the required practical you look for a link between an environmental factor and the distribution of a species. The **independent variable** is the factor you change or compare (for example distance along the transect, or shaded versus open areas). The **dependent variable** is the number (or % cover) of the species. You can do this with a transect (a gradient) or by comparing two areas, such as a shaded area and a sunny area, using random quadrats in each.

bullets: **Light intensity:** use a light meter (units: lux). Hold it at the same height, pointing the same direction, each time.
**Soil moisture:** use a soil moisture meter or compare the mass of a soil sample before and after drying.
**Soil pH:** use a pH probe, or soil indicator solution and a colour chart.
**Temperature:** thermometer or temperature probe, placed at the same depth or height each time.
**Wind speed:** an anemometer (units: m/s).
The reading is taken at the same place as the quadrat, so you can plot the plant count against the factor.
Digital data loggers and probes reduce human error and give more precise readings than estimating by eye.
core.p: To link distribution with an environmental factor you must measure the factor, not just guess. Each factor has a piece of equipment, and each measurement must be made at the same position as the quadrat so that the two sets of data can be paired. Readings should be repeated and averaged, because a single reading can be affected by passing clouds, shade or a damp patch.

bullets: Keep the **same quadrat size**, species, time of year and counting method.
Use the **same person** to count each quadrat if possible, to avoid differences in judgement.
Take readings on the same day and in similar weather where possible.
**Valid** = measures what it is supposed to measure and controls other variables. **Reliable** = repeated results are similar. **Accurate** = close to the true value.
Using more quadrats and repeating transects improves reliability.
Weakness: counting by eye can be inaccurate with plants that are small, overlapping or difficult to identify.
Improvement: use a larger number of quadrats, a smaller transect interval, or repeat in a different season.
core.h: Control variables, accuracy, validity and reliability
core.p: Examiners test whether you understand how to make the investigation a **fair test**. Only the independent variable should change; everything else that could affect the number of plants should be kept the same or monitored. Sampling investigations in the field are harder to control than lab experiments because the weather and the habitat cannot be controlled, so you must say that other factors may be varying.

bullets: **Ticks** (carry Lyme disease), stinging plants, brambles: wear long trousers and sleeves, check skin afterwards.
**Sun and heat:** use sun cream, a hat and take water, to avoid sunburn and dehydration.
**Slips, trips and uneven ground, long tapes and quadrats:** watch where you walk, stay with a group and take care when carrying equipment.
**Soil and animal faeces or dirty water:** wash hands thoroughly after fieldwork; cover cuts.
**Allergies and hay fever** to pollen: take medication, let the teacher know.
Do not remove plants or animals, do not trample, and keep to paths where possible. Return any animals moved to where they were found.
Follow the rule that you tell a responsible adult where you are and do not go in water or near roads without permission.
core.h: Safety, ethics and care of the environment
core.p: Fieldwork brings different hazards to the laboratory, so the risk assessment is part of the required practical. You should be able to name a hazard, say why it is a hazard and give a control. You also have a duty to leave the habitat as you found it, because the organisms you are studying are living things and the site may be protected.

bullets: **Table:** headings with units, the independent variable in the first column, repeated counts, then the mean.
**Line graph or scatter graph** for a transect: distance (or the abiotic factor) on the x-axis, mean number on the y-axis. A **bar chart** is used for comparing two separate areas.
Describe a trend with numbers, for example: as distance from the tree increases from 0 m to 20 m, the number of daisies per m2 increases from 1 to 10.
A trend between the two variables is a **correlation**: positive (both increase), negative (one increases while the other decreases) or none.
Correlation does not prove causation. Other factors, such as soil moisture, can change along the transect too.
Suggest improvements: more quadrats, more transects, measure more abiotic factors, repeat in other seasons.

Link to other topics: the ideas link to **competition**, **adaptations**, **photosynthesis** and **human impacts on biodiversity**, where sampling is used to monitor the effects of pollution and land use.
core.h: Processing, presenting and evaluating the data
core.p: After collecting the raw data you process it with the mean (and sometimes the median, mode and range) and then present it so that patterns are easy to see. A graph helps to show the correlation between distance and number of organisms, and the quality of the conclusion depends on how reliable and valid the data are. You should always refer to the data in the answer, using numbers.

exam: For a **method question** (4 or 6 marks) use a numbered sequence: lay two tapes as a grid, generate random coordinates, place the quadrat, count, repeat, calculate the mean, scale up.
Always use the phrases '**random number generator**', '**coordinates**', '**repeat**' and '**calculate a mean**' in sampling answers.
For 'why use random sampling?' write: '**to avoid bias**' or 'so the sample is representative'. For 'why repeat?': 'to improve reliability / identify anomalies'.
For a **calculation** show every step: mean, then per m2, then multiply by area. Marks are awarded for working even if the answer is wrong.
**2 mark** answers need two points: a statement plus a reason (for example 'more quadrats, so the mean is more reliable').
'Describe the trend' (command word **describe**): use figures from the graph with units and say if it increases, decreases or stays the same.
'Suggest' questions: apply biology to the context, for example link light to photosynthesis and growth.
For 'evaluate' or 'suggest improvements' say: more quadrats, more transects, same-sized quadrats, measure the abiotic factor, repeat in another season.
On graphs, check the **axes labels, units and scale** and plot points accurately with a ruler; draw a line of best fit only if the data suggest one.
Do not say the result 'proves' anything; use 'suggests', 'is correlated with' or 'is consistent with'.
Quote the numbers: examiners reward use of data from the table or graph.

mistakes.r: Use a random number generator to give coordinates on a grid made with two tape measures, so that there is no bias.
mistakes.w: Throw the quadrat over your shoulder / pick a spot at random by eye.

mistakes.r: Take many quadrats (at least ten), count in each and calculate a mean, to make the estimate reliable.
mistakes.w: Count the plants in one quadrat.

mistakes.r: Scale up: mean per m2 x the total area of the habitat in m2.
mistakes.w: Population = the mean number in a quadrat.

mistakes.r: Mean per quadrat / area of the quadrat. For 0.25 m2 you multiply by 4.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to divide by the quadrat area (0.25 m2) when finding the number per m2.

mistakes.r: A transect takes samples at regular (systematic) intervals along a line to show change along a gradient.
There is a correlation between light intensity and the number of daisies; other factors may also vary, so cause is not proven.
mistakes.w: The results prove that light causes more daisies.

mistakes.r: Use the same sized quadrat, the same species, the same time and the same counting method.
mistakes.w: Make it a fair test by using different sized quadrats.

mistakes.r: Name the hazard (for example ticks), say what harm it causes (Lyme disease), and give a control (long trousers, check skin).
mistakes.w: Only say 'it is dangerous' for safety.

summary: You need to know how to use **quadrats** and **transects** to estimate the **population size** and study the **distribution** of a species in a habitat, how to sample randomly and systematically, how to calculate means, population estimates and percentage cover, and how to link distribution to abiotic factors. It is a required practical, and questions on method, calculations and evaluation appear regularly on Paper 2.

terms.d: A square frame of known area placed on the ground to sample the organisms inside it.
A line laid across a habitat along which samples are taken at regular intervals to show how the distribution of organisms changes.
A small, representative part of a habitat that is studied in order to estimate what is happening in the whole habitat.
Choosing the positions of samples by chance, for example using random numbers, so that every part of the area has an equal chance of being sampled and bias is removed.
Taking samples at regular intervals, for example along a transect.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time.
A measure of how many individuals of a species there are, or how much area they cover.
Where in a habitat a species is found.
The percentage of the area of a quadrat that is covered by a species.
A non-living factor of the environment, such as light intensity, temperature or soil pH.
A living factor of the environment, such as competition, predation or disease.
Reflecting the whole habitat, so that the sample gives a fair estimate.
A systematic error that pushes the results in one direction, for example from choosing quadrat positions by eye.
Giving similar results when the investigation is repeated.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results.
A relationship between two variables; it does not by itself show that one causes the other.
The sum of all the values divided by the number of values.
The place where an organism lives.

worked.q: A student uses 10 quadrats (each 0.5 m x 0.5 m) in a field of area 600 m2 and counts daisies: 4, 7, 3, 5, 6, 2, 8, 5, 4, 6. Estimate the population of daisies in the field. (4 marks)
steps: Area of quadrat = 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 m2, so mean per m2 = 5 / 0.25 = 20

worked.ans: Daisies increase with distance from the tree, probably because light increases (correlation, other factors might also change); percentage cover = 32%
worked.q: Daisies were counted in 1 m2 quadrats along a 20 m transect from under a tree: 0 m = 1, 5 m = 3, 10 m = 6, 15 m = 9, 20 m = 10. Light intensity increased along the transect. Describe the pattern and suggest an explanation. (3 marks) A quadrat with 25 squares has the daisy covering 8 squares: calculate percentage cover. (2 marks)
steps: Pattern: the number of daisies per m2 increases from 1 to 10 as distance from the tree increases from 0 m to 20 m (positive correlation).
Explanation: light intensity increases away from the tree, so there is more light for photosynthesis, more glucose for growth, so more daisies survive.

worked.ans: Model answer: lay two tapes as a grid; generate random coordinates; place the quadrat at each; count dandelions inside; repeat at least 10 times; calculate the mean number per quadrat; convert to number per m2; multiply by the total area of the field to estimate the population.
worked.q: Describe how you would use quadrats to estimate the population size of dandelions on a school field. (6 marks)
steps: Mark the area using two tape measures laid at right angles to form a grid.
Use a random number generator to obtain pairs of coordinates.
Place a quadrat at each pair of coordinates, avoiding trampling.
Count the number of dandelions in the quadrat and record.
Repeat many times (at least 10) to make the data reliable.
Calculate the mean per quadrat, divide by the area of the quadrat to get the number per m2, then multiply by the total area of the field.
